description: Article-based learning cards with subtitle, body paragraphs, and takeaway.

cards.title: More Options Don't Make You Happier
cards.subtitle: 24 jam varieties attracted crowds. 6 varieties sold more jam.
body: The big display attracted more people. The small display sold ten times more jam.
Too many options creates paralysis. People walk away rather than choose wrong.
cards.takeaway: More options increase attraction but can decrease action.

cards.title: Maximizers vs Satisficers
cards.subtitle: People who seek 'the best' end up less satisfied than those who seek 'good enough.'
body:
• Maximizers research exhaustively and second-guess constantly
• Satisficers set a threshold and stop when they hit it
The maximizer found the best restaurant. The satisficer enjoyed dinner.
cards.takeaway: Seeking 'good enough' often produces more satisfaction than seeking 'the best.'

cards.title: Opportunity Cost Escalates
cards.subtitle: Every choice means giving up alternatives.
body: Chocolate or vanilla? You give up one thing. Thirty-one flavors? You give up thirty.
The more options you rejected, the more reasons you have to second-guess.
cards.takeaway: Abundant choice multiplies the things you didn't pick.

cards.title: Expectations Rise With Options
cards.subtitle: Limited options? Blame the options. Unlimited? Blame yourself.
body: One pair of jeans in your size—you buy it. Fifty pairs—you expect perfection.
With unlimited choice, anything less than perfect feels like your failure.
cards.takeaway: Unlimited options create expectations that reality can't meet.

cards.title: Regret and Reversibility
cards.subtitle: Decisions you can undo feel lighter—but get revisited forever.
body: Return policies seem like a gift. They're actually a trap—keeping the decision open.
Irreversible decisions hurt more upfront but create peace faster.
cards.takeaway: Reversible choices stay open; irreversible choices force closure.

cards.title: Adaptation Erases Perfect Choices
cards.subtitle: You found the perfect apartment. Six months later, it's just home.
body: Hedonic adaptation means we adjust to both good and bad. The thrill of the perfect choice fades.
The maximizer spent months searching. The satisficer spent a weekend. Both feel the same a year later.
cards.takeaway: Adaptation equalizes outcomes that felt vastly different at decision time.

cards.title: Social Comparison Poisons Satisfaction
cards.subtitle: Your new car felt great until your neighbor bought a better one.
body: More options means more comparison points. Social media shows everyone who chose differently.
Satisfaction isn't absolute—it's relative to what you're comparing against.
cards.takeaway: Comparison transforms good choices into inadequate ones.

cards.title: Choice Becomes a Burden
cards.subtitle: Freedom to choose should feel empowering. Sometimes it's just exhausting.
body: Decision fatigue is real. Every choice depletes a limited resource.
The freedom to optimize everything becomes the obligation to optimize everything.
cards.takeaway: Too much choice converts freedom into exhaustion.

cards.title: Constraints Can Be Liberating
cards.subtitle: Three menu options = enjoy dinner. Hundred options = work.
body: Constraints reduce decision load. Less energy choosing, more experiencing.
Artists work within constraints—the sonnet, the budget, the deadline. Constraints focus creativity.
cards.takeaway: Well-chosen constraints reduce burden and increase satisfaction.

cards.title: Satisficing Is a Skill
cards.subtitle: Knowing when good enough is good enough takes practice.
body: 'Good enough' sounds like settling. It's actually strategic.
Define your threshold in advance. Stop when you hit it. The discipline is in the stopping.
cards.takeaway: Satisficing is learnable and usually rational.

cards.title: Reduce Options Deliberately
cards.subtitle: Curation is kindness. Fewer options = better experience.
body:
• Restaurants with shorter menus
• Stores with curated selections
• Human recommendations over infinite catalogs
Someone already did the filtering. That's a service, not a limitation.
cards.takeaway: Curation adds value by removing options.

cards.title: The Paradox Is Solvable
cards.subtitle: Choice overload is a design problem with design solutions.
body: The paradox isn't an argument against freedom—it's for thoughtful choice architecture.
Defaults, recommendations, filters—these make abundant choice navigable.
cards.takeaway: Smart design can preserve choice while reducing its costs.
